simple return.def: The change in price over a period divided by the price at the start. A move from 100 to 120 dollars is a simple return of 20%.

growth factor.def: What one dollar at the start of a period became by its end: one plus the simple return. A 20% gain is a growth factor of 1.20.

compounding.def: The multiplying of growth factors over successive periods, so that each period's return is earned on the gains and losses of the periods before it.

e.def: The mathematical constant 2.71828, the amount one dollar grows to in a year at 100% interest compounded continuously. It is the base of the natural logarithm.

continuous compounding.def: Growth added in infinitely small, infinitely frequent amounts. At a rate r for t years, one dollar grows to e raised to the power r times t.

natural logarithm.def: The power to which e must be raised to give a number, written ln. It turns multiplication into addition: the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.

log return.def: The natural logarithm of a period's growth factor, the end price divided by the start price. Log returns are symmetric for a round trip and add up over time.

square-root-of-time rule.def: For independent returns with a constant variance, the standard deviation over n periods is the one-period standard deviation times the square root of n.

volatility.def: The annualized standard deviation of log returns, quoted as a percentage. A volatility of 20% corresponds to a typical daily move of about 1.26%.

geometric Brownian motion.def: The standard model of a price moving in continuous time, under which log returns over any period are normally distributed and independent of the past.

Black-Scholes model.def: The option pricing model, also called Black-Scholes-Merton, that values an option by assuming the underlying follows geometric Brownian motion and can be traded continuously to hedge it.

arithmetic mean.def: The ordinary average of a set of returns: their sum divided by how many there are. Over time it overstates what an investment compounds to.

geometric mean.def: The constant return per period that would compound to the same final value as the actual sequence of returns. It is what compounding actually delivers.

variance drag.def: The gap between the arithmetic mean return and the compound growth rate, about half the variance of returns. Also called the Ito drift correction.

concave function.def: A function whose graph bends downward, such as the logarithm. The average of its values at two points lies below its value at their average.

Kelly criterion.def: The rule for sizing a bet or position that maximizes the long-run compound growth rate of wealth, which is the same as maximizing the expected logarithm of wealth.

return distribution.def: The set of possible outcomes of a strategy or asset over a period, each weighted by its probability.

delta.def: The change in an option's value for a one-dollar move in the underlying. A 30-delta option gains or loses about 30 cents for each dollar the underlying moves.

put option.def: A contract giving its holder the right, not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price on or before expiry.

SPX.def: The S&P 500 index of large US companies, and the ticker of the cash-settled index options written on it.

premium.def: The price of an option, paid by the buyer to the seller when the trade is made.

strike price.def: The price at which an option's holder may buy the underlying, for a call, or sell it, for a put.

expiry.def: The date on which an option stops trading and is settled or lapses.

short volatility.def: A position that profits when the underlying moves less than option prices imply, usually built by selling options, and loses when it moves more.

moment.def: One of a series of averages that summarize a distribution. The mean is the first, the variance the second, and the standardized third and fourth are the skewness and the kurtosis.

skewness.def: The third standardized moment of a distribution, measuring its asymmetry. Negative skewness means a longer tail of losses than of gains; a normal distribution has zero.

kurtosis.def: The fourth standardized moment of a distribution, measuring how much weight sits in its extreme tails. A normal distribution has a kurtosis of 3.

excess kurtosis.def: Kurtosis minus 3, so that a normal distribution scores zero and a fat-tailed one scores above it.

CBOE PUT Index.def: A Cboe benchmark that tracks a strategy of selling at-the-money SPX puts each month, fully backed by cash. It has been tracked since June 1986.

at-the-money.def: Said of an option whose strike is at, or very close to, the underlying's current price.

fat tails.def: A distribution has fat tails when extreme outcomes are much more likely than a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation would make them.

value at risk.def: The return at a chosen percentile of the return distribution. The 95% value at risk is the return that is worse than 95% of outcomes.

expected shortfall.def: The average return in the part of the distribution beyond the value at risk, such as the worst 5% of months. Also called conditional value at risk.

stress scenario.def: A concrete hypothetical market move, such as the index falling 20% while the VIX rises 25 points, used to compute what a position would lose.

Sharpe ratio.def: A strategy's mean return above the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of its returns: the excess return earned per unit of volatility.

edge.def: The expected value of a trade or strategy, net of all costs. A trade has edge only if that number is positive.

breakeven win rate.def: The win rate at which a bet's expected value is exactly zero: the average loss plus costs, divided by the sum of the average win and the average loss.

expected utility.def: The probability-weighted average of the value a person places on each possible level of wealth. Maximizing it, rather than expected dollars, gives large losses the extra weight they deserve.

calendar spread.def: A position that sells an option at one expiry and buys an option of the same type and strike at a later expiry, profiting from how the two re-price over time.

payoff diagram.def: A chart of a position's profit or loss at expiry against the price of the underlying.

iron condor.def: A four-option position that sells a put spread below the price and a call spread above it. The short version profits if the underlying stays between the short strikes, and its loss is capped.

risk-free rate.def: The return on money lent to a safe borrower, usually the US government, for the period in question. Excess returns are measured above it.

Sortino ratio.def: Excess return divided by downside deviation, the standard deviation of returns below a threshold. It counts only shortfalls as risk.

information ratio.def: A strategy's average return above a benchmark divided by the standard deviation of that difference, its tracking error.

tracking error.def: The standard deviation of the difference between a strategy's returns and its benchmark's returns.

Calmar ratio.def: The mean annual return divided by the size of the maximum drawdown: return per unit of the worst peak-to-trough loss.

tail beta.def: A strategy's beta to the market measured only over the market's worst periods, such as its worst 5% of months.

alpha.def: Return beyond what a model's risk factors explain, often claimed as the reward for a manager's skill.

XSP.def: The Mini-SPX index option, one tenth the size of an SPX option.

probabilistic Sharpe ratio.def: The probability that a strategy's true Sharpe ratio exceeds a chosen threshold, given the observed Sharpe ratio, the number of observations and the skewness and kurtosis of the returns.

deflated Sharpe ratio.def: The probabilistic Sharpe ratio tested against the best Sharpe ratio that luck alone would produce across all the strategies tried, which corrects a backtest for selection.

VIX3M.def: Cboe's index of the implied volatility of S&P 500 options over the next three months, the longer-dated companion of the VIX.

realized volatility.def: The volatility an asset actually showed over a past period, computed from its returns and annualized.

survivorship bias.def: The distortion that comes from studying only the cases that survived, such as the markets or funds that still exist, and ignoring those that failed.

strangle.def: A position of a put and a call on the same underlying and expiry, with the put's strike below the price and the call's above it. Selling one is a bet that the price stays between the strikes.

SPY.def: An exchange-traded fund that tracks the S&P 500 index, and the ticker of the options written on it.
